sentence: The NHS describes metformin as a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes, and says it is usually the first choice prescribed for it.
note: NHS metformin page: usually the first medicine prescribed for type 2 diabetes.

sentence: It can also be used for gestational diabetes (diabetes in pregnancy) and for polycystic ovary syndrome, which the NHS pages call PMOS.
note: Summary: metformin can treat type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes and PMOS; PMOS expansion as returned.

sentence: Clinicians generally start it when diet and exercise alone have not been enough to control blood sugar.
note: Summary of NHS page.

sentence: The NHS says it works by helping the body respond better to insulin and by reducing the sugar the liver releases into the blood.
note: Summary: improves how body handles insulin; reduces sugar released by liver.

sentence: It is only available with a prescription.
note: Summary: only available with a prescription.

sentence: The NHS says metformin comes as two kinds of tablet: standard tablets and slow-release (modified-release) tablets.
note: NHS how-and-when page: 2 types of tablet.

sentence: Standard tablets act quickly and may need taking several times a day, while slow-release ones work gradually, so they are taken less often.
note: Summary of NHS page.

sentence: The NHS says the prescriber sets the amount, and that treatment is usually started small and built up slowly to limit side effects.
note: Summary: doses usually go up slowly to reduce side effects; the doctor sets tablets.

sentence: It says taking metformin with or just after a meal helps limit side effects, and that tablets are swallowed whole with water rather than chewed.
note: Summary: with or just after evening meal; swallow whole with water, not chewed.

sentence: For diabetes, the NHS says treatment is usually long term, and that stopping suddenly makes blood sugar rise.
note: Summary: usually for life; stopping suddenly makes blood sugar rise.

sentence: Because the NHS pages give different schedules for other uses, such as in children, the prescriber's instructions and the leaflet in the pack are the guide for any one person.
note: Summary: other NHS pages list different schedules for other uses.

sentence: The NHS lists nausea, being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain, loss of appetite and a change in taste among the common side effects.
note: Summary of main NHS page side-effect list.

sentence: It says most of these should ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine, although some can last longer.
note: Summary: most ease after a couple of weeks; some may last longer.

sentence: The NHS says taking the tablets with a meal and building up slowly can reduce them.
note: Summary: take with meal; start low and increase gradually.

sentence: If they remain too much, it says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets instead.
note: Summary: doctor may suggest switching to slow-release.

sentence: Diabetes UK also says stomach-related effects often go away within a few weeks, and that side effects can happen at any time during treatment, not only at the start.
note: Diabetes UK summary: often go within a few weeks; can happen anytime.

sentence: Diabetes UK advises people on standard-release tablets who have these effects to talk to their GP or diabetes team.
note: Diabetes UK summary.

sentence: The NHS says that taking metformin for a long time can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, which can make a person very tired.
note: Summary: long-term use can lower B12; deficiency can make you very tired.

sentence: Diabetes UK likewise says long-term use can lower vitamin B12 levels.
note: Diabetes UK summary: long-term metformin can lead to lower B12.

sentence: The NHS says a doctor may check B12 levels in the blood, and that vitamin B12 supplements help if levels are too low.
note: Summary: doctor may check B12; supplements help if too low.

sentence: Symptoms mentioned alongside deficiency include tiredness, muscle weakness and a sore, red tongue.
note: Search summary listed tiredness, weakness, sore red tongue as deficiency symptoms (page attribution to NHS common-questions page uncertain).

sentence: The NHS says that being ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or a high temperature while taking metformin carries a risk of dehydration, meaning the body loses too much water.
note: Summary: vomiting, diarrhoea or fever risk dehydration.

sentence: Other NHS guidance in the results says metformin may need to be paused during such illness and that the GP should be contacted.
note: Summary: temporarily stop when unwell and contact GP; the blended source was an NHS leaflet, so attribution to this page is uncertain.

sentence: On alcohol, the NHS says drinking is possible while taking metformin, but gives limits, because drinking more can raise the risk of low blood sugar.
note: Summary: can drink but keep to NHS limits; more can increase risk of low blood sugar.

sentence: An NHS trust leaflet adds that heavy drinking may raise the risk of lactic acidosis.
note: St George's NHS leaflet: excessive alcohol may increase risk of lactic acidosis.

sentence: The NHS says metformin may need to be stopped before surgery under general anaesthetic and before scans or tests that use an injected dye.
note: Summary: may need to stop before surgery and certain tests, including iodine-based dye scans.

sentence: It says the doctor will tell a person when to restart.
note: Summary of a St George's leaflet plus common questions page; attribution to NHS page is uncertain.

sentence: The NHS says most adults and children aged 10 and over can take metformin, but it is not suitable for everyone.
note: Summary of Who can and cannot take page.

sentence: Situations to raise with a doctor before starting include a past allergic reaction to metformin, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure or a recent heart attack, and heavy alcohol use.
note: Summary list from Who can and cannot take page.

sentence: The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, alone or with insulin, and usually while breastfeeding, after checking with a doctor.
note: Pregnancy page summary: can be taken; very small amounts in breast milk. The tool's wording 'safe' was not used.

sentence: It also says there is no evidence that metformin reduces fertility in men or women.
note: Summary of pregnancy/fertility page.

sentence: The NHS says not to take two doses to make up for a missed one.
note: Summary: do not take two doses to make up for missed one.

sentence: A pharmacist or GP is the usual route for questions about a missed dose or about side effects that do not settle.
note: Route to advice; NHS pages point to pharmacist/GP. Textbook-style signposting.

sentence: Lactic acidosis is a rare but serious side effect, and the NHS lists being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps and breathing problems as signs.
note: Summary: signs include vomiting, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for suspected lactic acidosis or a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).
note: Summary: call 999 for lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis.

sentence: For other serious side effects, it says to call NHS 111.
note: Summary: call 111 for other serious side effects.

sentence: NHS 111 is also the NHS route if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.
note: Summary: NHS page advises calling 111 if more than prescribed taken.
